extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, storytellers, film writers and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating film/story structure across the spectrum of archplot, miniplot, antiplot, multiplot and nonplot, including choices about agency, reality consistency, change vs stasis, and political/aesthetic positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Design Triangle / Structure Spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: All storytelling possibilities are distributed inside the story design triangle; each side of the triangle is a spectrum of structural choices (e.g., openness/closedness, passivity/activity, consistent/inconsistent reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are unlimited shades and degrees along these spectrums; writers slide their stories along these lines, blending or borrowing from each extreme. Very few works are pure examples of an extreme corner. Use the triangle to locate a work's balance among archplot, miniplot and antiplot and to decide which structural tensions to emphasize. Examples cited: THE FABULOUS BAKER BOYS, THE CRYING GAME (midway); BARTON FINK (draws from all extremes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archplot (Classical Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A classical, strongly structured plot typically featuring a single protagonist, active conflict with external forces, consistent reality, closed ending and a clear arc of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplot prioritizes strong causal order and decisive external action. Films that exemplify classical design (cited): CHINATOWN, THE SEVEN SAMURAI. Archplot tendencies produce stories that arc and show visible life-change for better or worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miniplot (Minimalistic/Inner Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimalistic form in which conflict is more interiorized; protagonists may be passive or isolates and endings may be open; change is subtle and often occurs at the deepest inner level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot leans toward inner conflict and minimal external resolution; change can be virtually invisible because it occurs internally. Examples: FIVE EASY PIECES, THE SCENT OF GREEN PAPAYA, 3 WOMEN, THE FABULOUS BAKER BOYS (halfway between archplot and miniplot). Note that miniplot works can still arc, but the arc is internal and understated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiplot (Antistructure / Self-reflexive Satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: A form characterized by inconsistent realities, fractured temporal and causal order, absurdity or satire, and an overall questioning of 'what's real'; often resists conventional arcing and closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiplot may employ devices (mockumentary elements, hallucination, surrealism) that break the audience's trust in the story's reality and push the work toward self-reflexivity or cosmic joke. Examples: BARTON FINK (moves from archplot to miniplot to antiplot), MONTY PYTHON AND THE HOLY GRAIL, LAST YEAR AT MARIENBAD. Use of false-reality scenes (e.g., WHEN HARRY MET SALLY faux-documentary interviews) can nudge a conventional story toward antistructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Works composed of multiple, interwoven storylines (an ensemble), occupying a middle ground between archplot and miniplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplot can be 'hard' (tending toward archplot with frequent turns and strong external consequences) or 'soft' (leaning toward miniplot with slowed pace and internalized action). Robert Altman's films are cited as masters of this form. Examples: NASHVILLE (hard multiplot), 3 WOMEN (soft multiplot). Consider how individual lines interact and whether they create a cohesive causal/ thematic whole or a looser mosaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonplot (Stasis / Portraiture / Slice-of-Life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that do not arc — life remains in stasis from opening to closing; these are narrative portraits or slice-of-life pieces rather than stories that show change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonplot can be realistic portraiture (verisimilitude) or absurdist/antistructured. Although they don't tell story in the classical sense, nonplots can inform and move us and offer insight that affects the audience. Examples: UMBERTO D, FACES, THE NAKED BOURGEOISIE, SHORT CUTS (malaise bookending the film). Recognize the distinction between creating narrative insight and designing plot-driven change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change versus Stasis (Classification Criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary axis: above the line are stories where life clearly changes (arc), below the line are stories that remain in stasis (non-arc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this axis to decide whether your narrative aims to produce a value-charged condition change in the protagonist's life (archplot/miniplot) or to hold life essentially the same (nonplot). Note that even at Miniplot's limits change may be almost invisible (inner change), while Antiplot's limits may produce absurd or cosmic transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist Agency: Active versus Passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choice whether the protagonist is active (driving events) or passive (reacting/isolated), which strongly influences whether a work leans toward archplot or miniplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active protagonists and external conflicts favor archplot; passive isolates and inner conflicts favor miniplot. Consider protagonist agency when shaping cause-effect chains and the audience's perception of momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality Consistency (Consistent versus Inconsistent Reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural choice about whether the story maintains a single, reliable reality or deliberately introduces inconsistent/false realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent reality supports conventional causal storytelling; inconsistent reality (e.g., mockumentary devices, hallucinations, scripted-as-documentary scenes) undermines stable causality and pushes toward antiplot. Example: WHEN HARRY MET SALLY inserts scripted 'documentary' interviews that question the film's reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and Causal Order (Linear versus Fractured)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story preserves normal chronology and cause-effect relations or fragments them into fractured temporal and causal sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fractured order destabilizes conventional plot expectations and is a hallmark of antiplot; stable order supports archplot's causal logic. Use this axis deliberately to shape audience understanding and thematic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending: Openness versus Closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between a closed, conclusive ending and an open ending that leaves futures unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archplot tends toward closed endings; miniplot and multiplot often leave endings open (examples: THE FABULOUS BAKER BOYS, THE CRYING GAME). Decide whether you want to resolve the value-charged condition or leave the protagonist's future ambiguous for thematic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics of Story Design (Hollywood vs Art Film / Aesthetic-Commercial Dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story design carries political and aesthetic implications — choices about stasis vs change and other structural axes map to debates about 'Hollywood film' versus 'art film' and to commercial versus artistic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of ideological biases and industry pressures: you may be tempted to design stories you don't truly believe in for commercial or festival reasons. 'Hollywood film' (as narrowly defined here) refers to a subset dominated by special-effects-driven pictures, farces and romances; 'art film' broadly refers to non-Hollywood (often European) films that achieve critical acclaim. Consider where your work fits and why; don't let external polemics trap your authentic design choices. Examples and counterexamples are given (REVERSAL OF FORTUNE, THE ACCIDENTAL TOURIST, BABETTE'S FEAST, IL POSTINO).
